justification: A tight-aggressive baseline for six-handed fixed-limit hold'em. When nobody has put money in yet we raise or fold; only the small blind sometimes completes, because it is already half in and only the big blind is left. Raising beats limping in limit: a raise sometimes wins the blinds at once, thins the field, and puts more money in while our hand is most likely ahead, and the raiser keeps the lead into the flop. Ranges widen as position improves, because fewer players behind us means fewer chances that someone holds a better hand, and acting last on every later street is worth extra hands. Facing one raise and no callers we mostly re-raise or fold; we call more often when callers or our own blind improve the price, and most of all in the big blind. Once two raises are in, the pot is large: when our own raise is re-raised we usually call with most of the hands we raised with; when none of the raises is ours we continue only with hands that are strong against one raise, and fewer of them; in both cases only premium hands raise again. Played over many hands, the chart aims to put money in voluntarily with about 18 to 26 percent of hands and to raise first with about 14 to 22 percent.

spots.justification: Five players still act behind us, so the chance that one of them holds a better hand is highest here. We open only hands that stay strong when called: pairs down to the middle, every suited ace, the best suited broadways and the top offsuit aces. Weaker offsuit hands are folded because they are easily dominated and we will usually play out of position.

We add pocket fours, a few more suited hands such as queen-nine, jack-nine and nine-eight, and more offsuit hands such as queen-jack and ace-nine. Everything we would open from the earlier seat is still a raise here.

spots.justification: Only the button and the two blinds remain, and the blinds will be out of position after the flop. A raise here often takes the blinds without a fight, so we open every pair, more suited kings and connectors, and offsuit aces down to about ace-seven. Hands that rely on hitting a big draw are still mostly left out, because the button can call or re-raise behind us.

spots.justification: Only the blinds can stop us, and we will act last on every later street. Stealing the blinds is now a big part of the profit, so we raise any ace, every suited king, offsuit kings down to about king-eight, connected suited hands and offsuit broadways. We still fold the weakest unconnected offsuit hands, which win too rarely when a blind calls and checks to us.

We raise a wide range of high-card hands to take the initiative and often win the blinds at once. Because we already have half a bet in, some weaker suited hands and suited connectors, plus queen-nine, jack-nine and ten-nine offsuit, complete instead: they are too weak to raise but cheap enough to see a flop.

spots.justification: A player in front of us has limped, which usually means a medium hand, and four players still act behind. We raise to isolate the limper with hands that play well heads-up: big pairs, strong aces and the best suited broadways. Small pairs, the smaller suited aces and the ten-high suited broadways prefer a cheap multiway flop, so they limp along hoping to hit a set, a flush or a straight.

spots.justification: With limpers in front and three players behind, we raise our stronger hands to punish the limps and to try for position against a single opponent. The limped pot gives good odds, so small pairs, the smaller suited aces and suited connectors from ten-nine down to seven-six over-limp: they win big when they connect and fold cheaply when they miss. Weak offsuit hands still fold.

We raise hands that are probably ahead of the limpers to build a pot we are favoured to win, even though we will act early after the flop. Everything else checks: a free flop costs nothing, and a weak hand can simply let the pot go later.

spots.justification: We limped, and a player behind us raised with nobody calling yet. A raise over our limp usually means a real hand, and anyone who limped after us still acts behind us. We re-raise only hands that do well against a raising range: jacks or better, ace-king and ace-queen suited, with jacks close to a call. Tens down to sevens, ace-queen offsuit, ace-jack suited and king-queen suited call one more bet because our limp is already in; everything else folds rather than playing a big pot without the lead.

spots.justification: Either the under-the-gun player opened and the rest folded to us, or we limped and a later player raised with nobody calling yet. Either way the raiser has shown strength. We re-raise to play heads-up with the initiative, using jacks or better, ace-king, ace-queen, ace-jack suited and king-queen suited; tens re-raise too but can also just call. A few middle pairs call to try to hit a set, and everything else folds, because those hands do poorly against a strong raising range and may face more raises.
